content_html_sanitized:
Source: http://www.marijuananews.com

Posted March 15, 2000
(MarijuanaNews note: I met Jacki at NORML’s National Medical Marijuana Day In 1994. She is confined to a wheelchair by a condition that causes her constant pain. I was amazed that someone so afflicted by pain could be so brave and bold. I saw her last year in Philadelphia, where she was a plaintiff in the medical marijuana Class Action suit.

Notice that the police went to her home at 11:45 at night, and stayed all night, showing no regard for her medical condition, which is obvious to even the most obtuse person. This is truly unconscionable!

By the way, when he was running for President in 1992, Bill Clinton promised Rickert that if he was elected he would see to it that she got medical marijuana. If he had won, things would surely be different.)



Report from a reader:
On March 13 at 11:45 pm, two Mondovi, WI police officers came to the door of Jacki Rickert, a 48-year-old disabled woman who lives with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, a degenerative connective-tissue disorder. They claimed they were there on a tip that she was in possession of marijuana and asked to search her home. When Ms. Rickert refused the request, they set about to procure a warrant (after initially telling her that they didn't need one as they were investigating a crime). After occupying her property for about 3 hours, the officers presented Ms. Rickert with a warrant to search for " marijuana, THC, Marinol, controlled substances and paraphernalia. "

The police spent the next 7 hours searching the home and belongings of Ms. Rickert, turning up an as-yet-undetermined quantity of marijuana and paraphrenalia. She was tentatively charged with possession with intent to deliver THC.
(MarijuanaNews note: This is truly insane. The woman is severely handicapped. Do they think that she uses her wheelchair to make deliveries?)

At approximately 10:00 am on 14 March, the officers disappeared from her house with their evidence, neglecting to inform her of her status, the status of the investigation, or a reason for leaving so quickly and quietly.

At 1:00 pm, they returned with paperwork, including the affidavit that launched the investigation. As of this post (14 March), the status of any possible case against her is unknown.

Jacki Rickert has smoked marijuana for years to cope with chronic pain as a result of her condition. She was accepted into a Federal investigational program which supplied a small number of chronically or terminally ill people with government-grown cannabis. However, the program was shut down before the Feds could fulfill their obligation. For the last 10 years, she has been a tenacious advocate for legal, medical use of cannabis.

From the NORML Weekly Press Release September 11, 1997

Second Medical Marijuana Wheelchair Trek Begins Today In Wisconsin

September 11, 1997, Modovi, WI - A seven-day, 210-mile wheelchair protest march for seriously ill patients who require medicinal marijuana but are legally denied access to it, begins today in Wisconsin. The demonstration, known as the " Journey for Justice II " will originate in Modovi and culminate at the state capitol. The inaugural journey took place in Ohio this past May.

The tour begins from the hometown of patient Jackie Rickert, who helped to organize the rally. Rickert, who suffers from Ehlors Danlos Syndrome, was approved by the federal government in 1990 to receive marijuana, but has never had her prescription honored. Thirteen additional patients will join Rickert on the eight town journey that concludes in Madison on September 18.

Upon arrival, Rep. Frank Boyle (D-Superior), along with co-sponsor Tammy Baldwin (D-Madison), will introduce legislation to protect patients who use marijuana under a physician's supervision from state criminal charges.

Event coordinator Kay Lee, who uses marijuana medicinally to treat severe rheumatoid arthritis, said that she hopes the second " Joumey for Justice " sends a strong message to state and federal politicians that there are thousands of seriously ill patients who benefit from the medicinal use of marijuana.

Lee also intends to drum up support for H.R. 1782, a federal bill in Congress that would remove federal restrictions that currently prevent physicians from legally prescribing marijuana.

" When common sense and compassion are in conflict with the law, then the law is wrong and must be changed, " she said.
From http://www.norml.org/news/archives/97-09-11.shtml
